title: Aeronautic Development Corp. (Jan 2017 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: Loss of the 35% Refundable Credit Through De Facto Control by a Non-Resident
summary: Aeronautic Development Corporation v. The Queen (2017 TCC 39) shows how Canadian SR&ED claimants can lose the 35% refundable investment tax credit available to CCPCs. The Tax Court of Canada held a U.S. resident and his U.S. corporation held de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) through economic dependence and non-arm's length dealings, denying ADC's 2009–2011 refundable credits.
metaDescription: Examine the January 2017 Tax Court of Canada decision for Aeronautic Development Corp. on Canadian SR&ED tax credit requirements.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2017 TCC 39, which was subsequently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2018 FCA 67 with leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed, stands as a landmark authority in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax jurisprudence. Presided over by Justice Robert J. Hogan under the General Procedure, the appeal addressed the critical intersection of corporate control mechanics, factual non-arm's length dealings, and cross-border contractual arrangements designed to access enhanced refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). While technical eligibility disputes under subsection 248(1) of the ITA frequently dominate SR&ED litigation, Aeronautic Development Corporation demonstrates that the most lucrative fiscal benefit of the Canadian SR&ED regime—the 35% enhanced ITC rate and 100% cash refundability reserved for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)—can be completely forfeited through structural governance and contractual failures before technical merits are even adjudicated.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Operational Context

The appellant, Aeronautic Development Corporation ("ADC"), was incorporated as a Nova Scotia unlimited corporation in April 2009 to carry out prototyping and certification work in the province of Quebec relating to the Seawind aircraft, an amphibious aircraft whose intellectual property rights were acquired by Richard Silva ("Mr. Silva"), a citizen and resident of the United States, after the failure of a Canadian company in which he had been an early investor. Mr. Silva completed the development of the Seawind amphibious aircraft in kit format, embarked on its "type" certification in the late 1990s, and controlled a United States corporation, Seawind Development Corporation ("Seawind Corp." or "Seawind"). According to Mr. Silva, he was approached by Investissement Québec and Industry Canada to carry out the certification work and the subsequent production of the Seawind in Quebec, and was advised by both agencies that he could become eligible to receive refundable SR&ED tax credits if the development work was carried out in Canada by a CCPC; after an initial Canadian structure, Flight Dynamics Corporation ("FDC"), encountered financial difficulty following the crash of the Seawind prototype during a test flight and went bankrupt, Mr. Silva acquired FDC's assets in 2009 to restart the certification program in Canada.

For its 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years, ADC filed SR&ED claims asserting status as a qualifying CCPC, thereby claiming refundable federal SR&ED ITCs pursuant to subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(1) of the ITA. ADC was initially wholly owned by Seawind Corp.; on August 17, 2009, ADC issued additional common shares such that, from that date until December 31, 2011, Seawind Corp. held 46% of its shares and voting rights, while the remaining 54% were held directly and indirectly by Canadian residents—7163860 Canada Inc. (44%, owned equally by ADC employees Patrick Desautels and Jean-François Bolduc), Aéro Manou Inc. (5%, controlled by ADC employee Manou Dessertine), and Patrick Desautels (5%) (the "Canadian Resident Shareholders"). Almost four months earlier, while ADC was still wholly owned by Seawind Corp., ADC had entered into a development agreement with Seawind Corp. (the "Development Agreement"), on terms dictated by Mr. Silva, to provide the prototyping and certification services on a cost-plus basis, with all resulting intellectual property belonging to Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., and Seawind Corp. remained ADC's sole client throughout the period. ADC maintained that subsection 256(5.1) did not apply because no non-resident person had any direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would have resulted in de facto control of ADC, given that Canadian residents held the majority of the voting shares from August 17, 2009 onward.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (the "CRA"), assessed ADC for the 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years and disallowed the refundable SR&ED ITCs in their entirety. The Minister's challenge rested on the premise that ADC was not a CCPC throughout the relevant taxation years because, from August 17, 2009 to December 31, 2011, it was controlled in fact (de facto control) by a non-resident person—namely, Mr. Silva, directly and through Seawind Corp. and Sea Air Composites ("Sea Air")—within the meaning of subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, the parties having agreed that before August 17, 2009 Seawind Corp. held de jure control of ADC through ownership of all of its shares, so that ADC was not a CCPC before that date.

The Crown advanced two positions to support the assessments. First, the Crown asserted that Mr. Silva, directly and through Seawind Corp. and Sea Air, exercised de facto control over ADC through economic influence derived from the Development Agreement and the parties' other commercial agreements and arrangements, which hung like a "Sword of Damocles" over the Canadian Resident Shareholders and was capable of influencing how they exercised their voting rights to determine the composition of, or a change in, the board of directors, and that the commercial-agreement exclusion in subsection 256(5.1) was unavailable because ADC and the alleged controller were not dealing at arm's length. Second, merely two weeks before the hearing and without amending its Reply, the Crown raised a new argument (the "New Argument") that the 44 common shares held by 7163860 Canada Inc. could not be voted until their subscription price was fully paid on March 9, 2012, so that Seawind Corp. held the majority of exercisable votes and ADC was controlled by a non-resident on both a de jure and a de facto basis throughout the relevant period.
Governing Statutory Framework

The legal dispute in Aeronautic Development Corporation is governed by an intricate web of statutory provisions within the ITA that regulate both the substantive eligibility of technical activities and the corporate control requirements for accessing enhanced SR&ED fiscal incentives. Under section 37 and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada was permitted, for the taxation years at issue, to deduct qualifying current and capital expenditures incurred for SR&ED (capital expenditures made after 2013 are no longer eligible). To qualify under the statutory definition in subsection 248(1), the underlying technical work must constitute basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement through a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis.

While, for the 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years at issue, standard corporate claimants earned a non-refundable 20% SR&ED ITC under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) to offset Part I tax otherwise payable (a general rate reduced to 15% for taxation years ending after 2013), subsection 127(10.1) granted an additional 15% ITC (20% since that reduction)—yielding an aggregate 35% enhanced rate—up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit exclusively to a corporation that was a CCPC throughout the taxation year. Furthermore, under subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2), a "qualifying corporation"—defined as a CCPC whose taxable income for the preceding taxation year, together with associated corporations, does not exceed the qualifying income limit—is entitled to a 100% cash refund of the 35% ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures. If a corporation fails to qualify as a CCPC, its ITC rate drops precipitously from 35% to the general rate (20% for the taxation years at issue in this case; 15% for taxation years ending after 2013), and its refundability drops to nil, rendering the credits entirely non-refundable and usable only as a carry-forward or carry-back against federal income tax payable.

The threshold gateway to this enhanced refundable regime is subsection 125(7) of the ITA, which defines a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation that is "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever," by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations described in paragraph (c), or by any combination of them. Paragraph (b) of the CCPC definition further aggregates all shares owned by non-resident persons and public corporations onto a single notional person to test whether they would hold de jure control.

To define the statutory phrase "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever," Parliament enacted subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, which establishes the regime of de facto control. Under subsection 256(5.1), a corporation is considered to be so controlled by another person or group of persons (the "controller") at any time where the controller has any direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of the corporation. This broad rule is subject to a narrow statutory saving clause where the corporation and the controller deal with each other at arm's length and the influence is derived under a franchise, licence, lease, distribution, supply, or management agreement, the main purpose of which is to govern the relationship between the parties regarding the manner in which a business carried on by the corporation is to be conducted. Complementing this rule is paragraph 251(1)(c) of the ITA, which stipulates that where persons are not legally related to each other by blood, marriage, or de jure corporate control, it is a question of fact whether they are at a particular time dealing with each other at arm's length. Finally, in response to the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 99 (and not in response to Aeronautic Development Corporation, whose taxation years it does not govern), Parliament enacted subsection 256(5.11) in 2017 through the Budget Implementation Act, 2017, No. 2, S.C. 2017, c. 33 (assented to December 14, 2017), applicable to taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017, to codify a broad, holistic statutory standard, mandating that the determination of de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) must take into consideration all relevant factors and need not include whether the taxpayer has a legally enforceable right or ability to effect a change in the board of directors or its powers, or to exercise influence over shareholders who have that right or ability.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Hogan dismissed ADC's appeal with costs, upholding the Minister's assessments for the 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years. As a preliminary matter, the Tax Court refused to consider the Crown's New Argument because doing so at that late stage, without an amendment to the Reply, would be a clear violation of procedural fairness, and added that the Crown had in any event failed to establish that any of ADC's common shares were non-voting during the relevant years; the appeal was therefore decided on de facto control. Applying the appellate standard for de facto control articulated in Silicon Graphics Ltd. v. Canada, 2002 FCA 260 and McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 99, Justice Hogan determined that Mr. Silva, had he chosen to do so, could have imposed his will on the Canadian Resident Shareholders, who held the legal power to elect the board of directors, with respect to the composition of, or a change in, ADC's board. Because ADC was economically dependent on Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva, and the Canadian Resident Shareholders were employees of ADC or entities owned by its employees, the Court found it unlikely that they would exercise their voting rights independently of Mr. Silva's wishes; and because ADC, Mr. Silva, and Seawind Corp. were not dealing at arm's length, the commercial-agreement exclusion in subsection 256(5.1) did not apply, so that Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. had de facto control over ADC pursuant to subsection 256(5.1), stripping ADC of its CCPC status under subsection 125(7) and invalidating its entitlement to refundable SR&ED ITCs. On April 4, 2018, the Federal Court of Appeal (2018 FCA 67) unanimously dismissed ADC's appeal with costs—although it held that the Tax Court had erred in relying in part on operational factors that McGillivray treats as irrelevant and in considering the parties' related status before August 2009, it found these errors immaterial because the Development Agreement was a legally enforceable supply agreement capable of conferring de facto control and the parties were not dealing at arm's length during the relevant period—and on March 7, 2019, the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed ADC's application for leave to appeal with costs.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of ADC's refundable SR&ED claims resulted from a convergence of ADC's economic dependence on Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva, non-arm's length dealings between ADC and Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., captive contractual dependencies under the Development Agreement, and the absence at trial of evidence of independent commercial viability.
Artificial Shareholding Architecture and Failure of Arm's Length Dealings

The foundational legal failure in Aeronautic Development Corporation was the taxpayer's reliance on a Canadian majority on its (de jure) share register while remaining economically dependent on, and not dealing at arm's length with, Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. Under the landmark common law test established in Buckerfield's Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue, [1965] 1 Ex. C.R. 299 and affirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 795, de jure control rests on the ownership of such a number of shares as carries with it the right to a majority of the votes in the election of the board of directors. ADC was not a CCPC before August 17, 2009 because Seawind Corp. held all of its shares; on that date ADC issued additional common shares so that Canadian residents held 54% of the shares and voting rights, either directly (Patrick Desautels, 5%) or through Canadian corporations owned by ADC employees (7163860 Canada Inc., 44%, and Aéro Manou Inc., 5%), against Seawind Corp.'s 46%.

However, Canadian jurisprudence under paragraph 251(1)(c)—anchored by the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Canada v. McLarty, 2008 SCC 26—evaluates three analytical criteria to determine whether unrelated parties deal with one another at non-arm's length in fact: first, whether there is a common mind which directs the bargaining for both parties to a transaction; second, whether the parties to a transaction are acting in concert without separate interests; and third, whether one party exercises de facto control over the other. Justice Hogan did not apply these criteria to the Canadian Resident Shareholders; his arm's length analysis instead concerned the relationship between ADC, on the one hand, and Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., on the other, and, considering the evidence as a whole, he found that they were not dealing with each other at arm's length in each of the relevant taxation years. ADC had nominal share capital: the Canadian Resident Shareholders' shares carried stated capital of only $1,100 (7163860 Canada Inc.), $125 (Aéro Manou Inc.), and $125 (Patrick Desautels), against $1,150 for Seawind Corp., and the $1,100 for the 44 shares of 7163860 Canada Inc. was, by administrative oversight, not paid until March 9, 2012. Conversely, ADC was entirely dependent on the cash flow provided by Seawind Corp. under the Development Agreement, all of its equipment belonged to Seawind Corp., and all intellectual property rights to the Seawind belonged to Mr. Silva or Seawind Corp. The Canadian Resident Shareholders were employees of ADC, or corporations owned by its employees, whose continued employment depended on ADC's financial viability; meanwhile, Mr. Silva alone defined the terms of the Development Agreement, ADC did not seek to renegotiate it when its initial 15-month term expired even though it was by then operating at a deficit, Mr. Silva unilaterally decided that the 5% Markup would not be paid without objection from ADC, and ADC operated out of a hangar belonging to Sea Air without a lease and with no evidence that it paid rent. Considering all of these circumstances, together with the fact that ADC and Seawind Corp. were related persons under paragraph 251(2)(b) of the ITA when the Development Agreement was entered into, the Court concluded that the requirement for arm's length dealings was not satisfied.
De Facto Control Under Subsection 256(5.1) and the McGillivray Standard

A critical legal tension in the appeal centered on the legal test for de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA. Prior to the 2017 enactment of subsection 256(5.11), the Federal Court of Appeal had narrowed the scope of subsection 256(5.1) in Silicon Graphics Ltd. v. Canada, 2002 FCA 260 and McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 99. Under the Silicon Graphics and McGillivray doctrine, operational or management control was irrelevant to establishing de facto control; rather, the putative controller had to possess a clear right and ability to effect a significant change in the board of directors or the powers of the board of directors, or "to influence in a very direct way the shareholders who would otherwise have the ability to elect the board of directors".

ADC argued that any economic influence had to be based on legal rights going beyond the ordinary commercial relationships of the parties, that it could and did operate independently of the alleged controller, and that its commercial arrangements with Seawind Corp.—principally the Development Agreement—were excluded from the Silicon Graphics test by the exclusionary language in subsection 256(5.1). Justice Hogan rejected this argument, reasoning that McGillivray confirmed that the list of relevant factors is open-ended, that the wording of the exclusion in subsection 256(5.1) shows that Parliament considered commercial agreements and arrangements capable of being a source of influence (so that, unless they fall within the narrow exclusion, they must be considered), and that control in fact exists where the evidence shows that the controller can affect the economic interest of the voting shareholders in a manner that allows the controller to impose his or her will on them, such that it would be unlikely that they would exercise their voting rights independently of the controller's wishes.

In evaluating the totality of the evidence, the Tax Court identified three reinforcing circumstances through which Mr. Silva could have imposed his will on the Canadian Resident Shareholders. First, there was profound economic dependence: ADC had nominal share capital, was entirely dependent on Seawind Corp.'s cash flow under a lopsided Development Agreement dictated by Mr. Silva, operated at a deficit, did not own its equipment, the resulting intellectual property, or its premises, offered no potential for earnings growth, and was unable to obtain funding from third parties, while the Seawind was to be manufactured and sold by Sea Air, another company controlled by Mr. Silva. Second, the Canadian Resident Shareholders were employees of ADC or entities owned by its employees, whose continued employment depended on ADC's financial viability; although the Court accepted that Ms. Dessertine was a competent manager who helped run ADC's operations, it held, following McGillivray, that operational or management control is irrelevant under the Silicon Graphics test, and it noted that Mr. Silva's own newsletters to investors described ADC's activities as those of an integrated, wholly owned organization. Third, Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. had what the Court called a "virtual stranglehold" on ADC's financial wellbeing: Seawind Corp. was ADC's sole client and the Development Agreement its sole source of revenue, Seawind Corp. withheld the Markup on Mr. Silva's instructions without objection from ADC, and when Seawind Corp.'s funding ceased in 2011, ADC suspended its operations, so that Mr. Silva, had he chosen to do so, could have imposed his will on the Canadian Resident Shareholders with respect to the composition of, or a change in, the board of directors. Furthermore, from a prospective advisory standpoint, the enactment of subsection 256(5.11) in 2017, which applies only to taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017 and therefore did not govern ADC's 2009 to 2011 taxation years, eliminates for later years the narrow legalistic defence ADC attempted to raise. Under subsection 256(5.11), courts are now statutorily required to consider all factors that are relevant in the circumstances when assessing de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), and a finding of control in fact no longer requires proof that the non-resident had a legally enforceable right or ability to change the board of directors or its powers, or to exercise influence over the voting shareholders who have that right or ability.
Captive Contractual Architecture and the Failure of the Subsection 256(5.1) Saving Provision

Beyond shareholder mechanics, ADC's contractual structure suffered from a fatal defect that precluded reliance on the statutory saving clause in subsection 256(5.1); the Court did not, however, rule on the eligibility of ADC's underlying SR&ED expenditures. Subsection 256(5.1) contains a specific carve-out providing that where a corporation and another person deal with each other at arm's length and the influence is derived under a franchise, licence, lease, distribution, supply, or management agreement—the main purpose of which is to govern the relationship between the parties regarding the manner in which a business carried on by the corporation is to be conducted—the corporation shall not be considered to be controlled in fact solely because of that agreement.

ADC argued that the Development Agreement fell within this exception, but the Court held that a commercial agreement is excluded only if (i) the corporation and the controller are dealing at arm's length at the relevant time and (ii) the main purpose of the agreement is to govern their relationship regarding the manner in which the corporation's business is carried on, and it found the first condition unmet. First, the saving provision in subsection 256(5.1) applies only where the corporation and the influencer deal with each other at arm's length; because Mr. Silva, Seawind Corp., and ADC were found not to be dealing with each other at arm's length in each of the relevant taxation years, the contractual carve-out was unavailable. Second, having found the arm's length condition unmet, the Tax Court did not need to rule on the main-purpose condition and made no finding that the Development Agreement's main purpose was to harvest tax credits (the Federal Court of Appeal later agreed with ADC that the Development Agreement was a supply agreement within the meaning of subsection 256(5.1)). ADC had no other clients, owned no intellectual property in the Seawind aircraft, and led no evidence that it had, or could find, certification and prototyping work from other aircraft developers.

In addition, captive cross-border R&D contracts create severe vulnerabilities under the substantive SR&ED expenditure and contract payment rules in subsections 37(1), 127(9), and 248(1) of the ITA. Under the definitions of "qualified expenditure" and "contract payment" in subsection 127(9), where a taxpayer performs SR&ED for or on behalf of another person, contract payments received from a person resident in Canada or carrying on business in Canada through a permanent establishment reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures to prevent double-claiming. While payments received from a non-resident corporation such as Seawind that is not carrying on business in Canada generally do not constitute a disqualifying "contract payment" under subsection 127(9)—thereby allowing a legitimate Canadian R&D contractor to claim SR&ED ITCs even when funded by a foreign client—this statutory architecture is strictly policed by the CRA under subsections 125(7) and 256(5.1) to prevent non-residents from artificially manufacturing CCPC status to extract 35% refundable cash subsidies from the Canadian treasury. Moreover, where a Canadian R&D entity deals at non-arm's length with its foreign parent or principal under a captive contract, billing arrangements, intercompany loans, and unpaid R&D fees trigger rigorous scrutiny under section 67 (general limitation as to reasonableness of expenses), subsection 78(1) (unpaid amounts in non-arm's length transactions), and section 247 (transfer pricing adjustments).
Evidentiary, Technical, and Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies

At trial before the Tax Court of Canada, the initial burden of demolishing the Minister's factual assumptions rests squarely on the taxpayer. ADC's evidentiary presentation suffered from critical documentation and credibility deficits that sealed the dismissal of its appeal. Specifically, ADC led no evidence that it had, or could find, work from other clients, and its evidence that Ms. Dessertine helped manage its operations was held irrelevant because operational or management control does not establish independence under the Silicon Graphics test; moreover, its 2009 and 2010 financial statements disclosed, under the heading "economic dependence", that the Development Agreement was its sole source of revenue, a note that was dropped from the 2011 statements prepared after the CRA audit had commenced. Furthermore, Mr. Silva testified that Investissement Québec and Industry Canada had advised him that he could become eligible for refundable SR&ED tax credits if the development work was carried out in Canada by a CCPC, and that he had hired a major Canadian accounting firm to advise him on a structure giving access to those credits; the Court did not, however, find that the Canadian Resident Shareholders were inserted solely as a façade, deciding the case instead on economic dependence and non-arm's length dealings.

Finally, the record showed that Mr. Silva travelled regularly to ADC's workplace and oversaw the work it carried out, although the Court did not rule on the technical eligibility of that work as SR&ED. In aerospace experimental development—which requires rigorous adherence to the five-question jurisprudential test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (98 DTC 1839), encompassing technological uncertainty, explicit hypothesis formulation, systematic investigation via experiment or analysis, technological advancement, and contemporaneous record-keeping—the record indicates that the technical direction of the Seawind aircraft project rested with Mr. Silva, who had acquired the Seawind's intellectual property and, in 2009, the technical database of the earlier Canadian certification program carried out by FDC. When a Canadian subsidiary cannot demonstrate through contemporaneous technical logs, project charters, and engineering authority matrices that its own Canadian-resident leadership independently formulated the scientific hypotheses and directed the experimental methodology, the evidentiary record weakens the SR&ED claim on its technical merits, although under the McGillivray standard applied in this case such operational or technical control is not, on its own, determinative of de facto control under subsection 256(5.1).
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Aeronautic Development Corporation and the governing Canadian SR&ED framework against the specific deficiencies exhibited by the taxpayer and the evidentiary standard of proof demanded by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Aeronautic Development Corp.
Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Benchmark

cells: Qualification as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC)
ITA s. 125(7); s. 127(10.1); s. 127.1(1)–(2)
ADC claimed the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC rate reserved for CCPCs despite being controlled in fact by a U.S. resident (Mr. Silva) and his U.S. corporation (Seawind).

The taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that throughout the entire taxation year, no non-resident person(s) or public corporation(s) held de jure or de facto control, either alone or as a notional group.
Arm's Length Dealings Between the Corporation and the Alleged Controller
ITA s. 251(1)(c), s. 251(2)(b); Peter Cundill & Associates Ltd. v. R., [1991] 1 C.T.C. 197 (FCTD); Canada v. McLarty, 2008 SCC 26

ADC, Mr. Silva, and Seawind Corp. were found not to be dealing at arm's length: Mr. Silva alone set the terms of the Development Agreement, ADC did not renegotiate it after its 15-month term despite operating at a deficit, Mr. Silva unilaterally withheld the 5% Markup without objection, and ADC occupied Sea Air's hangar without a lease; the Canadian Resident Shareholders (employees or their corporations) held shares with nominal stated capital.

Requires objective, contemporaneous proof of independent bargaining, separate economic interests, genuine capital at risk, and absence of a single directing mind orchestrating both sides of the shareholding relationship.
Absence of Non-Resident De Facto Control (Pre-2017 Standard)
ITA s. 256(5.1); Silicon Graphics, 2002 FCA 260; McGillivray, 2016 FCA 99

Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. held a stranglehold on ADC's financial wellbeing through ADC's economic dependence (nominal share capital, sole client, sole revenue source under the Development Agreement, deficits, no ownership of IP or equipment), making it unlikely that the Canadian Resident Shareholders, who had the legal power to elect the board of directors, would vote independently of Mr. Silva's wishes.

Even without a formal Unanimous Shareholder Agreement (USA), de facto control is found where the evidence shows that the controller can affect the economic interest of the voting shareholders so as to impose his or her will on them, making it unlikely that they would vote independently of the controller's wishes; operational or management control is irrelevant.
Absence of Non-Resident De Facto Control (Post-2017 Expanded Standard)

Not applied in the decision: s. 256(5.11) applies only to taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017, so ADC's 2009–2011 years were decided under the pre-2017 McGillivray standard; had ADC's captive dependence on a single non-resident client (Seawind) and financier (Mr. Silva) arisen in a later year, it would be assessed under the broader s. 256(5.11) standard.

The Court evaluates all relevant operational, financial, IP, and contractual factors holistically; proof that the non-resident cannot alter the board of directors is no longer sufficient to rebut de facto control.
Exemption for Commercial Supply, Licensing, or Management Contracts
ITA s. 256(5.1) (Statutory Saving Provision)

The Development Agreement between Seawind Corp. and ADC was not between parties dealing at arm's length during the relevant years, so the exclusion did not apply; the Tax Court made no finding on the agreement's main purpose (the FCA later accepted that it was a supply agreement).

The taxpayer must prove both (1) factual arm's length status between the contracting entities under s. 251(1)(c), and (2) that the main purpose of the agreement is to govern the relationship between the corporation and the controller regarding the manner in which the corporation's business is carried on (client diversification and market-rate terms being advisable supporting evidence).
Autonomous Systematic Investigation & Contemporaneous SR&ED Documentation
ITA s. 37(1); s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839

Not adjudicated: the Court did not rule on the technical eligibility of ADC's work as SR&ED; the record showed only that Mr. Silva regularly visited and oversaw ADC's prototyping and certification work, and that the resulting intellectual property belonged to Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp.

Requires dated, contemporaneous technical documentation generated during the taxation year proving that qualified Canadian personnel identified technological uncertainties, formulated hypotheses, executed systematic testing, and logged time autonomously.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To assist Canadian tax counsel, corporate structurers, and R&D technical advisors in navigating the strict legal boundaries established in Aeronautic Development Corporation, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how projects confronting identical legal and technical vulnerabilities can be restructured to achieve full statutory compliance under the ITA.
Case Study 1: Cross-Border Aerospace Avionics and Composite Airframe R&D in Quebec
Initial Vulnerable Fact Pattern and Legal Pitfalls

AeroVance Systems Inc. ("AeroVance US"), a Delaware corporation wholly owned by a U.S. resident aerospace entrepreneur ("Dr. Vance"), has developed a prototype hybrid-electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) commuter aircraft. Encountering severe weight-to-thrust and de-icing delamination challenges during cold-weather flight testing, Dr. Vance incorporates a Quebec subsidiary, AeroVance Québec Inc. ("AVQ"), in Montreal to perform composite wing-skin curing and fly-by-wire avionics integration. Seeking to claim the 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC under subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(1) of the ITA alongside refundable Quebec R&D tax credits, Dr. Vance issues 49% of AVQ's Class A voting shares to AeroVance US—together with 100% of non-voting Class B preferred shares representing $4.5 million in seed funding—and issues 51% of the Class A voting shares for $510 in total to two Montreal-based aerospace consultants who work on the project. AVQ enters into an exclusive cost-plus-5% R&D services contract with AeroVance US, under which AeroVance US retains all background and foreground intellectual property, approves all weekly engineering sprints, and serves as AVQ's sole source of revenue. Furthermore, no formal hypothesis logs are maintained in Montreal; instead, engineers upload raw CAD files and finite element analysis (FEA) outputs directly to AeroVance US's server in Delaware.

Under Aeronautic Development Corporation (2017 TCC 39 and 2018 FCA 67) and subsection 256(5.11) of the ITA, this structure is fatally flawed. The two Montreal consultants paid nominal consideration of $510 and work on a project wholly funded by Dr. Vance, which (as with ADC's employee-shareholders) makes it unlikely that they would exercise their voting rights independently of Dr. Vance's wishes, while AVQ's relationship with AeroVance US would likely fail the factual arm's length test in paragraph 251(1)(c) on which the saving provision in subsection 256(5.1) depends. Consequently, Dr. Vance and AeroVance US exercise de facto control over AVQ under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) through direct shareholder influence, 100% preferred equity financing concentration, and a single-client contractual monopoly, destroying CCPC status under subsection 125(7). Simultaneously, the absence of localized, systematic experimentation documentation threatens the underlying SR&ED expenditure deduction and ITC claim under subsection 248(1) and section 37.
Step 1: Restructuring Project and Corporate Governance

To insulate the Canadian entity from reassessment and satisfy the Tax Court's evidentiary standards, the taxpayer must first dismantle the nominal shareholding façade prior to the commencement of the taxation year and replace it with bona fide, arm's length Canadian institutional or entrepreneurial equity ownership. Rather than issuing 51% of the voting shares for a nominal $510, AVQ must be capitalized through a substantive equity investment at fair market value by an arm's length Canadian aerospace venture capital fund or independent Canadian engineering co-founders who invest substantial, at-risk capital—such as $2.5 million in common voting equity—priced via an independent third-party valuation report. Both common and preferred shares must carry genuine economic participation rights so that voting power aligns directly with economic risk.

Concurrently, AVQ must constitute a five-member Board of Directors in which three directors are independent Canadian residents appointed by the Canadian voting shareholders, and only two are appointed by AeroVance US. Corporate counsel must draft a comprehensive Unanimous Shareholder Agreement (USA) under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Business Corporations Act (Quebec) that explicitly vests operational budget approval, executive hiring and termination, and strategic R&D project selection in the Canadian majority board, without granting Dr. Vance or AeroVance US veto rights over ordinary-course business or board composition. Alternatively, if Dr. Vance refuses to surrender de facto operational and economic control—which under subsection 256(5.11) will inevitably trigger non-resident control if AVQ remains economically dependent on AeroVance US—tax counsel must advise AVQ to file transparently as a non-CCPC. As a non-CCPC, AVQ remains fully eligible to deduct 100% of current SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) and claim the non-refundable 15% federal SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(5) against Part I tax payable generated from profitable intercompany engineering markups, while simultaneously claiming the refundable Quebec tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization (CRIC), which replaced the Quebec R&D salary tax credit for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 and does not impose the federal CCPC gatekeeping requirement for refundability.
Step 2: Restructuring Contract Terms and Intellectual Property Ownership

To neutralize the captive single-client trap that doomed ADC in Aeronautic Development Corporation and to satisfy the commercial saving provision in subsection 256(5.1), AVQ's contractual relationships must be thoroughly commercialized. AVQ must be transformed from a captive cost-centre into an independent Canadian aerospace R&D centre of excellence that bids on and executes composite material and avionics R&D contracts for multiple unrelated Canadian and international aerospace Tier-1 suppliers. Removing the single-client monopoly eliminates the existential economic threat that gave Mr. Silva de facto control over ADC.

Furthermore, the captive cost-plus service contract with AeroVance US must be replaced with an arm's length Joint Technology Development and Licensing Agreement negotiated by separate legal counsel for each entity. Under this restructured agreement, AVQ retains legal and beneficial ownership of all Canadian foreground intellectual property relating to cold-weather composite delamination resistance and grants AeroVance US a field-of-use commercial licence in exchange for market-rate milestone payments and royalties benchmarked via a contemporaneous Section 247 Transfer Pricing Study.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To satisfy the substantive definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, AVQ must establish an autonomous technical documentation architecture in Montreal that is clearly separated from routine U.S. product engineering. At the inception of each fiscal year, AVQ's Montreal engineering leadership must draft a formal SR&ED Technical Project Charter that explicitly segregates excluded routine Transport Canada and FAA airworthiness certification testing from qualifying experimental development. This charter must define the specific system-level technological uncertainty—specifically, the inability of standard autoclave curing profiles and epoxy resin matrices to prevent micro-cracking and electro-thermal de-icing layer delamination under rapid thermal cycling between −45°C and +120°C at high vibrational loads. Prior to each experimental phase, the Montreal Lead Aerospace Engineer must document explicit, quantifiable scientific hypotheses to be tested, such as formulating the hypothesis that modifying the graphene-nanotube doping concentration between 0.8 wt% and 1.4 wt% within the intermediate modulus carbon-fibre prepreg will alter the interlaminar shear strength and coefficient of thermal expansion sufficiently to eliminate delamination across 500 thermal shock cycles.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Contemporaneous Evidence

To substantiate that the systematic investigation occurred under Canadian technical direction, AVQ must implement a localized Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and electronic laboratory notebook system hosted and managed in Montreal. Every experimental iteration—including composite coupon fabrication Batch 1 through Batch 18, ultrasonic non-destructive evaluation results, failure mode analyses, and reformulated curing hypotheses—must be contemporaneously date-stamped and signed off by AVQ's Canadian Chief Technology Officer during the taxation year. In parallel, AVQ must deploy a bi-weekly time-tracking ledger that requires engineers and technicians to allocate hours directly to specific experimental hypothesis identifiers rather than generic corporate billing codes, rigorously separating eligible experimental testing and analysis from ineligible routine CAD drafting or administrative reporting.
Case Study 2: Clean-Tech Solid-State Battery Management and Powertrain R&D Subsidiary in Ontario
Initial Vulnerable Fact Pattern and Legal Pitfalls

VoltCore GmbH ("VoltCore Germany"), a German automotive supplier, seeks to develop an ultra-fast-charging solid-state battery thermal management system (BTMS) for heavy-duty electric mining trucks. To leverage Canadian clean-tech engineering talent and SR&ED tax incentives, VoltCore Germany's Chief Executive Officer ("Mr. Weber", a German resident) arranges for his former university colleague, a Canadian resident mechanical engineer living in Waterloo, Ontario ("Mr. Singh"), to incorporate VoltCore Canada Inc. ("VCI"). Mr. Singh subscribes for 100% of VCI's common voting shares for $100. However, VoltCore Germany extends a $6.0 million non-interest-bearing loan to VCI that is repayable on demand with a 15-day notice period, secured by a general security agreement (GSA) over all of VCI's assets and intellectual property. Furthermore, Mr. Singh signs an undocumented side letter agreeing to transfer his voting shares to VoltCore Germany for $100 upon request. VCI claims $1.8 million in refundable SR&ED ITCs as a CCPC for its first two taxation years. During the CRA audit, VCI provides high-level marketing slide decks summarizing the battery pack's final performance specifications, but cannot produce test bench logs showing failed thermal runaway trials or independent board minutes.

Under the principles of Aeronautic Development Corporation (2017 TCC 39), McGillivray, and subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) of the ITA, VCI faces certain reassessment and total disallowance of its refundable ITCs. The $6.0 million demand loan coupled with a GSA over all corporate assets, combined with the $100 nominal share capitalization and secret side letter, gives VoltCore Germany absolute economic life-or-death power over VCI and direct control over Mr. Singh, constituting de facto control under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) and non-arm's length dealing under paragraph 251(1)(c). Additionally, presenting only final marketing specifications without contemporaneous records of systematic experimental failure and analysis fails the Northwest Hydraulic evidentiary standard under subsection 248(1).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Debt Instruments

To eliminate non-resident de facto control under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) and establish genuine CCPC status under subsection 125(7), VCI must immediately terminate and void any formal or informal option, side letter, or nominee arrangement. VCI must be recapitalized so that Mr. Singh and a syndicate of arm's length Canadian clean-tech angel investors or venture funds hold 65% of the voting and participating equity at fair market value, supported by documented independent legal representation during share subscription negotiations to prove factual arm's length dealing under paragraph 251(1)(c).

Crucially, VCI must eliminate the existential financial leverage created by the non-resident demand loan. The $6.0 million 15-day demand loan from VoltCore Germany must be replaced with a combination of non-dilutive Canadian commercial bank financing or government clean-tech innovation grants—carefully accounting for the reductions for government assistance required under subsection 127(18) of the ITA—and a committed 7-year subordinated term credit facility carrying objective, market-standard financial covenants rather than an arbitrary demand feature. Canadian tax jurisprudence confirms that a non-arm's length demand loan capable of bankrupting the debtor at the lender's whim is a primary indicator of de facto control under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11). VCI must also establish a quarterly Board of Directors governance cadence in Waterloo where strategic budgets, commercial partnerships with Canadian mining operators, and R&D roadmaps are debated, voted upon, and recorded in detailed corporate minute books maintained by Canadian corporate counsel.
Step 2: Restructuring Contract Terms and Funding Exclusions

To qualify for the statutory saving provision in subsection 256(5.1) and avoid funded research disqualifications, VCI must structure its commercial relationship with VoltCore Germany as an arm's length Master R&D Collaboration and Commercial Supply Agreement. Under this agreement, VCI develops proprietary phase-change dielectric cooling technology for the global heavy-mining sector on its own account, while granting VoltCore Germany non-exclusive European distribution rights. Because VCI is contractually and commercially free to license and sell its BTMS hardware directly to Canadian mining enterprises, the contract qualifies as an authentic commercial supply and distribution agreement under the saving provision of subsection 256(5.1). Furthermore, all customer contracts must contain explicit payment schedules that segregate commercial product milestone payments from any domestic "contract payments" or "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), ensuring that VCI bears the genuine financial risk of cost overruns and experimental failures during the R&D phases.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To overcome the evidentiary deficiency of relying on high-level marketing slides, VCI must re-architect its technical documentation around the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1). Before initiating bench trials, VCI's Waterloo engineering team must compile a State-of-the-Art Engineering Baseline Dossier documenting why existing liquid-glycol and standard dielectric immersion cooling architectures fail when subjected to 4C continuous charge rates in solid-state lithium-metal cells—specifically identifying how dendritic short-circuiting is induced by localized thermal gradients exceeding ΔT > 4.5°C across the solid electrolyte interface. This dossier must isolate the exact technological advancement sought—creating new thermodynamic engineering knowledge regarding the phase-transition kinetics of two-phase fluoroketone micro-channel cooling under high-current transient loads—rather than framing the project around commercial product marketing targets.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Audit-Ready Evidence Integration

To build an unassailable evidentiary record for CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), VCI must configure its Waterloo battery cycler and thermal chamber test benches to automatically archive time-series telemetry data—including thermocouple arrays, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and pressure drop curves—linked to discrete experimental test runs such as Experiment Series BTMS-04A through BTMS-04M. Following each test bench anomaly or thermal runaway failure, the Waterloo R&D team must author a contemporaneous Experimental Analysis and Hypothesis Revision Memorandum within 48 hours of the test. This memorandum must explicitly record the hypothesis tested, the empirical test parameters, the observed divergence from predicted thermodynamic models, the scientific conclusion drawn, and the modified parameter matrix for the subsequent experiment. Finally, VCI's accounting controller must cross-reference every general ledger SR&ED expenditure—including T4 engineering salaries, subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) materials consumed or transformed during destructive battery cell testing, and arm's length Canadian testing subcontractors—directly to the corresponding Experiment Series identifier, creating a unified financial-to-technical audit trail.
Conclusion

The ruling of the Tax Court of Canada in Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2017 TCC 39, affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2018 FCA 67, delivers an unequivocal warning to cross-border enterprises and Canadian tax practitioners: entitlement to enhanced refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits cannot be manufactured through cosmetic share registers. Where Canadian resident voting shareholders hold nominal equity and depend for their employment on a corporation that is economically dependent on a non-resident who controls its funding, intellectual property, and sole source of revenue, the Tax Court will look past de jure share ownership to find non-resident de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), and the commercial-agreement exclusion will be unavailable where the corporation and the non-resident are found, as a question of fact under paragraph 251(1)(c), not to be dealing at arm's length; for taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017, subsection 256(5.11) further broadens the factors that may be considered. To safeguard SR&ED claims under the Income Tax Act (Canada), corporations must align substantive Canadian equity risk, independent board governance, diversified commercial contracts, and rigorous contemporaneous experimental documentation into a unified, audit-ready compliance framework.
